rationale: This is a mechanical ensemble of the archive's two top performers built from the same underlying `xrd`/`aqc` series, so the "partly independent measurement error" claim is doubtful and the outcome will be largely bounded by the two parents — a cosmetic blend rather than a new mechanism.

A strict ablation of an already-evaluated signal and therefore low in novelty, but it is a cheap, decisive attribution test of whether the R&D leg carries any incremental content, and the expression matches the hypothesis; note the coarse 0–5 integer leg and that `COALESCE(aqc,0)` conflates missing with genuinely zero acquisition activity.

R&D-to-assets and capex-to-assets are both long-published anomalies and their difference plus a profitability level is close to a linear recombination of known factors, and the tangible/intangible mix is dominated by sector membership rather than capital-allocation choice, so the "falsification test" framing does not rescue it from being a rediscovery.

A defensible diagnosis-driven repair whose IND_ZSCORE genuinely alters the ordering rather than being monotone-neutral, though it remains one operator away from an already-failed archive signal and leaves the profitability leg un-neutralized, so the asymmetry may limit interpretability of a null result.

The two legs are conceptually and mechanically distinct from prior variants (margin *trend* rather than asset-yield level, paired with acquisition intensity), the sign follows naturally from the expression, and the substitution is motivated by an actual precision result in the archive; watch for instability of TREND on a sales-deflated ratio when sales are small or negative.

Internally consistent — both legs load positively on the "failed acquirer," so the negative expected sign is correct — and the flow-based reformulation with a same-signed rank sum is a reasonable fix for the weak slope of the goodwill version, but it sits close to two existing archive signals (serial acquisitiveness and goodwill-validation) and to the published acquirer-underperformance literature, limiting how much genuinely new information it can deliver.
